As the NSW government prepares to approve an energy-from-waste facility on Wiradjuri Country, local Indigenous groups have not been properly consulted and fear its impacts on health and sacred sites.

Later this year, the New South Wales government is expected to approve a plant near Parkes that will generate energy by burning garbage trucked in from Sydney.

Consultation has been under way for seven years, but Indigenous groups have been excluded from recent rounds, adding to fears the project will affect human health, impact the environment and damage sacred sites. An earlier proposal in Western Sydney was rejected on health grounds, which precipitated the plan in the Parkes Special Activation Precinct (SAP) in the state’s Central West.

“This monstrosity they want to put there, it’s got to go,” says Frances Robinson, chair of the Peak Hill Local Aboriginal Land Council.

“My concern is health, contamination of Country that will also affect the farmers and their economy, and our bush tucker. Now they’re talking about the yellow box gum tree. That’s a medicinal tree to us. And there is supposedly a scar tree and some artefacts right there on the site.”

At a public hearing of an inquiry by the Select Committee on Proposed Energy from Waste Facilities, held in Parkes in April, Karryn Schaefer, chair of the Peak Hill Bogan River Aboriginal Advisory Committee, expressed concerns over the impact of emissions from the plant on nearby sacred sites. “Snake Rock is a culturally significant and protected site. We also have Bulgandramine Mission … where there are traditional graves and burial trees,” she said. “This site, like others, sits within the impact pathway of this proposal.”

Development of the Parkes SAP began in July 2018, and planning to include an energy-from-waste facility (EfW) began in May 2019. An international consortium called Parkes Energy Recovery (PER) was awarded a contract to develop and operate the facility in March 2025, under a land lease arrangement with Regional Growth NSW Development Corporation (RGDC).

In its submission to the parliamentary inquiry, Parkes Shire Council expressed doubts over the NSW government’s response to a 2020 report, released by NSW chief scientist and engineer Professor Hugh Durrant-Whyte, that recommended stricter safety controls and monitoring procedures for EfW proposals across the state.

“Council’s position is clear and uncompromising: if EfW facilities can operate safely, then the NSW Government must provide the evidence to prove it,” the council submitted. “If they cannot, then such facilities must not proceed, anywhere in the State.”

Shortly afterwards, the council passed a formal resolution rejecting the development of the EfW.

Asked what consultation there had been by the NSW government with her land council over the EfW, Robinson’s response was simple: “None. Not a blessed thing.”

Both Schaefer and Michael James, chair of the Parkes Aboriginal Community Working Party, echoed Robinson’s sentiments at the April public hearing.

Asked about consultation, James said: “None at all.”

Schaefer concurred: “We were not properly consulted by the proponents of this project. Free, prior and informed consent was not achieved. We are not opposed to progress, but it must not come at the cost of our existence.”

The NSW Departments of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure and of Primary Industries and Regional Development have been instrumental in the development of the precinct and the EfW.

Between 2018 and 2022, the two departments reached out to Wiradjuri community members five times. Consultation centred on determining the potential harm the precinct could have on Aboriginal objects and places through the creation of an Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Management Plan.

Since June 2022, however, there has been no consultation between the two departments and Wiradjuri community members regarding the facility or the development of the EfW within it.

“This monstrosity they want to put there, it’s got to go. My concern is health, contamination of Country that will also affect the farmers and their economy, and our bush tucker.”

This is despite promises from RGDC that the NSW government would “continue to work closely with Parkes Shire Council, stakeholders, and the community” while PER applied for its relevant planning and environmental approvals for the EfW.

As part of these approvals, the PER consortium is relying on the Aboriginal cultural heritage plan developed by the government for the site.

Ed Nicholas, the development chief executive of Tribe Infrastructure Group, the leading company in the PER consortium, says the NSW government “undertook an extensive Aboriginal heritage assessment report back in 2019, and subsequently a cultural heritage management plan. We as a tenant in their precinct are entitled to take advantage of the primary work they’ve done, and they’ve done extensive primary work.”

However, a freedom of information request revealed Heritage NSW, the government agency responsible for protecting cultural and environmental heritage, has repeatedly questioned the thoroughness of the Aboriginal cultural heritage plan and the broader consultative efforts of both the departments of planning and of regional development.

Between July 2022 and August 2023, Heritage NSW raised concerns with both departments about areas within the precinct not surveyed under the cultural heritage plan and warned that Aboriginal consultation remained inadequate, recommending further dialogue “with the identified Registered Aboriginal Parties (RAPs) for the Parkes SAP to identify, document and manage cultural heritage values”.

FOI documents showed the departments took no apparent steps to remedy these issues.

The department of planning also failed to include any Registered Aboriginal Parties in an email sent to stakeholders on January 6 this year, requesting input into the secretary’s environmental assessment requirements, a criterion intended to ensure proposals address all necessary environmental, social and economic impacts throughout approval processes for major projects.

Two weeks later, Heritage NSW again raised concerns with the department regarding a scoping report lodged by the consortium to begin the EfW’s approvals process. It stated the PER consortium’s environmental impact statement should be informed by an addendum to the cultural heritage plan, which “must include evidence of adequate and continuous consultation with Aboriginal parties”.

When questioned on the matter, Nicholas said the Aboriginal cultural heritage plan was being updated by the NSW government. However, he was unaware what changes were being made and how these responded to concerns raised by NSW Heritage.

“It’s really a matter for them to manage that. I think that’s a matter for you to discuss with heritage and planning.”

Both the departments of planning and of regional development declined to answer questions regarding their consultative efforts and Heritage NSW’s recommendations.

The department of planning also failed to respond to questions regarding a potential conflict of interest, given it has held consultative responsibilities with community members and is now the department responsible for assessing PER’s developmental and environmental applications.

PER has conducted its own consultation process including, according to Nicholas, three meetings with the Peak Hill Local Aboriginal Land Council, and one meeting with the Parkes Aboriginal Community Working Party in October 2025.

The land council was given less than a week’s notice to consult with their community for their second and final meeting with PER, in June 2025, after opposing the facility in an initial meeting.

“If they had given us 14 days’ notice, we could have got the word out to all the members of the land council to come and listen and have their say,” says Robinson.

At the April public hearing, Michael James from the Parkes Aboriginal Community Working Party raised concerns about PER’s request to meet just one day before submissions to the parliamentary inquiry closed. Consequently, he declined the meeting.

“I just thought the timing wasn’t very great to present whatever they were going to present. We were one day out from a chance to put a submission for or against the project.”

Wiradjuri people are also disappointed with the level of consultation conducted by the council regarding the EfW.

“For more than 11 years, Parkes Shire Council and Northparkes Mines employed a Parkes Shire Aboriginal Project Officer to represent and work with the Aboriginal community of Parkes and Peak Hill,” Jada Read, a Wiradjuri woman from Upper Bogan River Country, wrote in her submission to the parliamentary inquiry. “She was involved in the SAP consultations, yet she was never informed that an incinerator project was being proposed meaning she could not take this information back to our people for discussion or consent.”

Parkes Shire Council first learnt of the potential inclusion of an EfW within the Parkes SAP in May 2019, under former mayor Ken Keith. Keith declined to comment on consultation conducted with Wiradjuri community members throughout his mayorship.

Current mayor Neil Westcott said the council’s capacity to consult with the community regarding the EfW had been limited by its having been left in the dark by the NSW government.

“This is where the disappointment comes with the state government,” he says. “It’s the state government that should have been out here sitting down with our First Nations people. We simply don’t have information. I’ve had very little to share. The ministers would say otherwise.”

The EfW is in the final stages of its developmental and environmental assessments.

The Parkes Energy Recovery consortium is expected to exhibit findings from the assessment to the public in August or October.

Katherine Everest is a freelance journalist.
